source_text:
Tum sic Caecilius exorsus est: Quamquam tibi, Marce frater, de quo cum maxime quaerimus non sit ambiguum, utpote cum diligenter in utroque uiuendi genere uersatus repudiaris alterum, alterum conprobaris, in praesentiarum tamen ita tibi informandus est animus, ut libram teneas aequissimi iudicis nec in alteram partem propensus incumbas, ne non tam ex nostris disputationibus nata sententia quam ex tuis sensibus prolata uideatur.
proinde si mihi quasi nouus aliqui et quasi ignarus partis utriusque considas, nullum negotium est patefacerè, omnia in rebus humanis dubia, incerta, suspensa, magisque omnia uerisimilia quam uera.
quo minus miram est nonnullos taedio inuestigandae penitus ueritatis cuilibet opinioni temere succumbere quam in explorando pertinaci diligentia perseuerare.
itaque indignandum omnibus, indolescendum est audere quosdam, et hoc studiorum rudes, litterarum profanos, expertes artium etiam sordidarum, certum aliquid de summa rerum ac maiestate decernere, de qua tot omnibus saeculis sectarum plurimarum usque adhuc ipsa philosophia deliberat.
nec inmerito, cum tantum absit ab exploratione diuina humana mediocritas, ut neque quae supra nos caelo suspensa sublata sunt, neque quae infra terram profunda demersa sunt, aut scire sit datum aut scrutari permissum aut suspicari religiosum, et beati satis satisque prudentes iure uideamur, si secundum illud uetus sapientis oraculum nosmet ipsos familiarius nouerimus.
sed quatenus indulgentes insano atque inepto labori ultra humilitatis nostrae terminos euagamur et in terram proiecti caelum ipsum et ipsa sidera audaci cupiditate transcendimus, uel hunc errorem saltem non uanis et formidulosis opinionibus implicemus.
sint principio omnium semina natura se coeunte densata, quis hic auctor deus? sint fortuitis concursionibus totius mundi membra coalita, digesta, formata, quis deus machinator ? sidera licet ignis accenderit et caelum licet sua materia suspenderit, licet terram sua fundauerit pondere et mare licet confluxerit e liquore, unde haec religio, unde formido?
quae superstitio est? homo et animal omne quod nascitur, inspiratur, attollitur, elementorum ut uoluntaria concretio est, in quae rursum homo et animal omne diuiditur, soluitur, dissipatur: ita in fontem refluunt et in semet omnia reuoluuntur, nullo artifice nec iudice nec auctore.
sic congregatis ignium semmibus soles alios atque alios semper splendere, sic exalatis terrae uaporibus nebulas semper adolescere, quibus densatis coactisque nubes altius surgere, isdem labentibus pluuias fluere, flare uentos, grandines increpare, uel nimbis conlidentibus tonitrua mugire, rutilare fulgora, fulmina praemicare: adeo passim cadunt, montes inruunt, arboribus incurrunt, sine dilectu tangunt loca sacra et profana, homines noxios feriunt et saepe religiosos.
quid tempestates loquar uarias et incertas, quibus nullo ordine uel examine rerum omnium impetus uolutatur? in naufragiis bonorum malorumque fata mixta, merita confusa? in incendiis interitum conuenire insontium nocentiumque? et cum tabe pestifera caeli tractus inficitur, sine discrimine omnes deperire? et cum belli ardore saeuitur, meliores potius occumbere?
m pace etiam non tantum aequatur nequitia melioribus, sed et colitur, ut in pluribus nescias, utrum sit eorum detestanda prauitas an optanda felicitas.
quod si mundus diuina prouidentia et alicuius numinis auctoritate regeretur, numquam mereretur Phalaris et Dionysius regnum, numquam Rutilius et Camillus exilium, numquam Socrates uenenum.
ecce arbusta frugifera, ecce iam seges cana, iam temulenta uindemia imbri corrumpitur, grandine caeditur. adeo aut incerta nobis ueritas occultatur et premitur, aut quod magis credendum est, uariis et lubricis casibus soluta legibus fortuna dominatur.
thought_title: Caecilius opens: human knowledge is uncertain, so no one should decide about God
orientation: Caecilius begins his speech to Marcus, asking him to act as a fair judge and arguing that all human affairs are doubtful and uncertain.
pass_a_gloss: Then Caecilius began thus: Although for you, brother Marcus, the matter about which we are especially inquiring is not doubtful, since you have diligently lived in each manner of living and have rejected the one and approved the other, nevertheless for the present your mind must be shaped in such a way that you hold the balance of a most fair judge and do not lean inclined into one part, lest the opinion seem not so much born from our disputations as brought forth from your own feelings. Therefore if you sit with me as someone new and as someone ignorant of each part, it is no trouble to make clear that all things in human affairs are doubtful, uncertain, hanging, and all things more probable than true. By which it is less strange that some people from weariness of investigating truth deeply yield rashly to any opinion whatever than that they persevere in searching with persistent diligence. And so all must be indignant, all must grieve, that certain people dare, and these people untaught in studies, profane in letters, lacking experience even of common arts, to decide something certain about the highest reality and majesty, about which up to now philosophy itself with so many sects in all ages deliberates. And not without reason, since human mediocrity is so far from divine investigation that neither the things which are raised up above us, suspended in heaven, nor the things which are sunk deep below the earth, have been given to know or permitted to search or religious to suspect, and we seem happy enough and wise enough by right, if according to that old oracle of the wise man we know ourselves more intimately. But insofar as we, indulging an insane and inept labor, wander beyond the limits of our lowliness and, thrown upon the earth, transcend heaven itself and the stars themselves with bold desire, let us at least not entangle this error with empty and fearful opinions. Let the seeds of all things at the beginning be packed together by nature coming together with itself: who is this author god? Let the limbs of the whole world have grown together, been arranged, been formed by chance collisions: who is the god contriver? Although fire may have kindled the stars and although heaven may have hung itself by its own matter, although it may have founded the earth by its own weight and although the sea may have flowed together from liquid, whence is this religion, whence is this fear? What superstition is this? Man and every animal that is born, is breathed into, is raised up, is a voluntary coming together of elements, into which again man and every animal is divided, dissolved, scattered: thus they flow back into the source and all things are rolled back into themselves, with no maker nor judge nor author. Thus when seeds of fires have been gathered, other and other suns always shine, thus when vapors of the earth have been breathed out, mists always grow, and when these have been packed and forced together, clouds rise higher, and when these fall, rains flow, winds blow, hailstones rattle, or when storm clouds collide, thunder roars, lightnings flash red, thunderbolts flash forth: so they fall everywhere, they rush upon mountains, they run into trees, without distinction they touch sacred and profane places, they strike guilty men and often religious men. Why should I speak of the varied and uncertain storms, by which the assault of all things is rolled about with no order or examination? In shipwrecks the fates of good and bad men are mixed, their merits confused? In fires the destruction of innocent and guilty comes together? And when the tract of heaven is infected with pestilential decay, all perish without distinction? And when it rages with the heat of war, the better men rather fall? In peace also wickedness is not only made equal to better men, but is even cultivated, so that in most cases you do not know whether their detestable depravity or their desirable happiness is to be chosen. But if the world were ruled by divine providence and by the authority of some deity, Phalaris and Dionysius would never deserve a kingdom, Rutilius and Camillus would never deserve exile, Socrates would never deserve poison. Behold fruitful trees, behold now the white harvest, now the drunken vintage is spoiled by rain, is cut down by hail. Thus either uncertain truth is hidden from us and pressed down, or, what is more to be believed, fortune, released from laws, rules by varied and slippery chances.

choices.why: Glossary term; Caecilius uses it dismissively of religious fear, and the fixed rendering preserves the debate's key vocabulary.
Glossary term; Caecilius asks whence religion and fear arise, and the fixed rendering keeps the contrast with superstition.
Glossary term; Caecilius denies that the world is ruled by divine providence, and the fixed rendering preserves the argument's key term.
Glossary term; Caecilius refers to the authority of some deity, and the fixed rendering keeps the pagan divine power sense.
Caecilius concludes that fortune, released from laws, rules by chance; 'fortune' preserves the personified force he opposes to providence.
Caecilius says the fates of good and bad men are mixed in shipwrecks; 'fates' keeps the plural noun and the sense of allotted outcomes.

pass_b_english: Then Caecilius began: "Although for you, Marcus my brother, the question we are about to examine is not in doubt—since you have lived carefully in both ways of life and have rejected one and approved the other—still, for the present you must shape your mind so that you hold the balance of a most impartial judge and do not lean in favor of one side. Otherwise your verdict will seem to come not from our arguments but from your own prior feelings.

So if you sit with me as someone new and ignorant of both sides, it is no trouble to show that everything in human affairs is doubtful, uncertain, and hanging in suspense, and that all things are more probable than true.

That makes it less surprising that some people, weary of searching out truth to the bottom, surrender recklessly to whatever opinion comes along rather than persist with stubborn diligence in investigating.

And so everyone should be indignant and aggrieved that certain people—untaught in these studies, ignorant of literature, ignorant even of the lowliest crafts—dare to pronounce something certain about the highest reality and majesty, about which philosophy itself, through so many centuries and so many schools, is still deliberating.

And rightly so, since human smallness falls so far short of divine inquiry that we are not permitted to know or search out the things suspended above us in the sky, nor the things sunk deep beneath the earth, nor is it even religious to guess at them. We would rightly seem blessed enough, and wise enough, if according to that old saying of the wise man we came to know ourselves more intimately.

But insofar as we indulge this insane and foolish labor and wander beyond the limits of our lowliness, and though cast down upon the earth we reach beyond heaven itself and the very stars with audacious desire, let us at least not entangle this error with empty and fearful opinions.

Let the seeds of all things be, in the beginning, compressed by nature coming together on its own—what god is the author here? Let the parts of the whole world have coalesced, been arranged and shaped by random collisions—what god is the designer? Grant that fire lit the stars, that heaven hangs suspended by its own material, that earth is founded on its own weight and the sea has flowed together from liquid—where does this religion come from, where does this fear?

What superstition is this? Man and every animal that is born, breathes and is raised up is a voluntary coming together of the elements, and into those elements man and every animal is again divided, dissolved, and scattered. So all things flow back to their source and return into their own source, with no maker, no judge, no author.

Thus when the seeds of fire are gathered, different suns always shine, one after another; thus when vapors are exhaled from the earth, mists are always rising; when these are thickened and pressed together, clouds rise higher; as they glide along, rains flow, winds blow, hail rattles, or when storm clouds collide, thunder roars, lightning flashes, and thunderbolts blaze forth.
Indeed they fall everywhere, crash into mountains, strike trees, touch sacred and profane places without distinction, kill guilty men and often the religious.

Why should I speak of the varied and uncertain storms, by which the onrush of all things is tumbled about with no order or judgment? In shipwrecks the fates of good and bad men are mixed, their merits confused? In fires destruction falls upon innocent and guilty alike? And when the sky's region is infected with deadly plague, everyone perishes without distinction? And when war rages with fury, it is the better men who fall?
In peace too, wickedness is not only made equal to better men, but is even honored, so that in most cases you cannot tell whether their depravity should be detested or their good fortune desired.

But if the world were ruled by divine providence and the authority of some deity, Phalaris and Dionysius would never have met with a kingdom, Rutilius and Camillus would never have met with exile, Socrates would never have met with poison.

Look: fruit-bearing trees, look: the already whitening crop, the already drunken vintage is ruined by rain and cut down by hail. So either the truth is hidden from us and suppressed, or—what is more believable—fortune, loosed from all laws, rules by varied and slippery chances."

fixed: inspiratur means 'breathes in', not 'is breathed into'; changed to 'breathes and is raised up'.
in semet omnia reuoluuntur: semet refers to the source/elements, not 'themselves'; changed to 'return into their own source'.
soles alios atque alios semper splendere: 'different suns one after another', not 'one sun after another'; changed to 'different suns always shine, one after another'.
nebulas semper adolescere: nebulas = mists, not clouds; changed to 'mists are always rising'.
rerum omnium impetus uolutatur: impetus = onrush, not 'assault'; changed to 'the onrush of all things is tumbled about'.
in incendiis interitum conuenire insontium nocentiumque: conuenire = 'falls upon', not 'comes together'; changed to 'destruction falls upon innocent and guilty alike'.
meliores potius occumbere: 'it is the better men who fall', not ambiguous 'the better rather fall'; changed.
aequatur nequitia melioribus: melioribus = 'better men', not abstract 'the better'; changed to 'better men'.
numquam mereretur: mereretur = 'would have met with', not 'deserved'; changed all three instances.
iam temulenta uindemia: temulenta = 'drunken', not 'ripening'; changed to 'the already drunken vintage'.
premitur: 'hidden and buried', not 'kept down in uncertainty'; changed.
soluta legibus: 'loosed from all laws', not 'released from laws'; changed.

fixed.note: The English repeats 'hidden' ('hidden from us and hidden and buried'), and 'premitur' means suppressed; the fix reads 'is hidden from us and suppressed', which avoids the doubled word that the checker's fix would leave.

dismissed.why: Latin describes a ripe harvest, not a drunken one.
dismissed.note: 'Temulenta' really does mean 'drunken'; Minucius uses it as a picture of grapes swollen with wine, and 'drunken vintage' keeps that picture rather than misstating it.

dismissed.why: Missing 'bonorum malorumque' (of good and bad men); 'fata' alone loses the key contrast.
dismissed.note: The English already says 'the fates of good and bad men are mixed', so nothing is omitted.

dismissed.why: 'Melioribus' = 'to the better' (abstract/neuter), not 'better men'; 'nequitia' is subject, 'wickedness is made equal to better things/virtues'.
dismissed.note: 'Melioribus' refers to better people, as the following 'eorum' (their depravity, their good fortune) shows, so 'better men' is correct.

dismissed.quote: the already whitening crop, the already drunken vintage
dismissed.why: 'Cana' = 'white/gray' (ripe with grain), 'temulenta' = 'swelling/ripe'; both describe ripeness, not intoxication.
dismissed.note: 'Whitening crop' correctly renders 'cana', and 'drunken' is a fair literal rendering of the wine-filled image in 'temulenta'.
